pieces.about: A watch is a portable timepiece intended to be carried or worn by a person. It is designed to keep a consistent movement despite the motions caused by the person's activities. A wristwatch is designed to be worn around the wrist, attached by a watch strap or other type of bracelet, including metal bands, leather straps, or any other kind of bracelet. A pocket watch is designed for a person to carry in a pocket, often attached to a chain.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon

pieces.name: Waterfall
pieces.about:
A waterfall is any point in a river or stream where water flows over a vertical drop or a series of steep drops. Waterfalls also occur where meltwater drops over the edge 
of a tabular iceberg or ice shelf.

also.title: Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs

pieces.name: Water polo
pieces.about: Water polo is a competitive team sport played in water between two teams of seven players each. The game consists of four quarters in which the teams attempt to score goals by throwing the ball into the opposing team's goal. The team with more goals at the end of the game wins the match. Each team is made up of six field players and one goalkeeper. Excluding the goalkeeper, players participate in both offensive and defensive roles. It is typically played in an all-deep pool where players cannot touch the bottom.

pieces.name: Wax seal
pieces.about: A seal is a device for making an impression in wax, clay, paper, or some other medium, including an embossment on paper, and is also the impression thus made. The original purpose was to authenticate a document, or to prevent interference with a package or envelope by applying a seal which had to be broken to open the container.

pieces.name: Wheelchair
pieces.about: A wheelchair is a mobilized form of chair using 2 or more wheels, a footrest and armrest usually cushioned. It is used when walking is difficult or impossible to do due to illnesses, injury, disabilities, or age related health conditions.

also.title: The Coffee Bean for Kids: A Simple Lesson to Create Positive Change

pieces.name: White laboratory coat
pieces.about: A white coat, also known as a laboratory coat or lab coat, is a knee-length overcoat or smock worn by professionals in the medical field or by those involved in laboratory work. The coat protects their street clothes and also serves as a simple uniform. The garment is made from white or light-colored cotton, linen, or cotton polyester blend, allowing it to be washed at high temperature and making it easy to see if it is clean.

pieces.name: Wikipedia
pieces.about: A free online encyclopedia written and edited by volunteers, launched in 2001.

also.title: How I Built This - Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales

pieces.name: William Morris
pieces.about: William Morris was an English textile designer, poet, artist, writer, and socialist activist associated with the British Arts and Crafts movement. He was a major contributor to the revival of traditional British textile arts and methods of production. His literary contributions helped to establish the modern fantasy genre, while he helped win acceptance of socialism in fin de siècle Great Britain.

pieces.name: Wine
pieces.about: Wine is an alcoholic drink made from fermented grape juice

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
To Someone from A Warm Climate (Uiscefhuaraithe)

pieces.name: Wool hat
pieces.about: Wool is the textile fiber obtained from sheep and other mammals, especially goats, rabbits, and camelids. The term may also refer to inorganic materials, such as mineral wool and glass wool, that have some properties similar to animal wool.

pieces.name: World Wide Web (The Web)
pieces.about: The World Wide Web is an information system that enables content sharing over the Internet through user-friendly ways meant to appeal to users beyond IT specialists and hobbyists. It allows documents and other web resources to be accessed over the Internet according to specific rules of the Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP).

also.title: How I Built This - Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales

pieces.name: X-ray
pieces.about: X-rays are a form of high-energy electromagnetic radiation. In many languages, it is referred to as Röntgen radiation, after the German scientist Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen, who discovered it in 1895 and named it X-radiation to signify an unknown type of radiation.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon

pieces.name: Zodiac
pieces.about: The zodiac is a belt-shaped region of the sky that extends approximately 8° north and south of the ecliptic, the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere over the course of the year. Also within this zodiac belt appear the Moon and the brightest planets, along their orbital planes. The zodiac is divided along the ecliptic into 12 equal parts ("signs"), each occupying 30° of celestial longitude. These signs roughly correspond to the astronomical constellations with the following modern names: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.

The September 11 attacks, commonly known as 9/11, were four coordinated Islamist terrorist suicide attacks carried out by al-Qaeda against the United States in 2001. On that morning, 19 terrorists hijacked four commercial airliners scheduled to travel from the East Coast to California. The hijackers crashed the first two planes into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City and aimed the next two flights toward targets in or near Washington, D.C., in an attack on the nation's capital. The third team succeeded in striking the Pentagon, the headquarters of the U.S. Department of Defense in Arlington County, Virginia, while the fourth plane crashed in rural Pennsylvania during a passenger revolt. The September 11 attacks killed 2,977 people, making it the deadliest terrorist attack in history. In response to the attacks, the United States waged the multi-decade global war on terror to eliminate hostile groups deemed terrorist organizations, as well as the foreign governments purported to support them, in Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, and several other countries.

pieces.name: Boot camp
pieces.about: Military recruit training, commonly known as basic training or boot camp, refers to the initial instruction of new military personnel. It is a physically and psychologically intensive process, which resocializes its subjects for the unique demands of military employment.

pieces.name: Crusades
pieces.about: A series of religious wars fought between 1095 and 1291, called and supported by the Latin Church, chiefly to take and hold Jerusalem and the Holy Land.

also.title: Life During the Crusades
also.year: 1998 (Library of Congress record and copyright date c1998; Goodreads and some retailer listings say 1997 - see dropped.md)

pieces.name: Eleusinian Mysteries
pieces.about: The Eleusinian Mysteries were initiations held every year for the cult of Demeter and Persephone based at the Panhellenic Sanctuary of Eleusis in ancient Greece. They are considered the "most famous of the secret religious rites of ancient Greece". Their basis was a Bronze Age agrarian cult, and there is some evidence that they were derived from the religious practices of the Mycenean period. The Mysteries represented the myth of the abduction of Persephone from her mother Demeter by the king of the underworld Hades, in a cycle with three phases: the descent (loss), the search, and the ascent, with the main theme being the ascent of Persephone and the reunion with her mother. It was a major festival during the Hellenic era, and later spread to Rome. Similar religious rites appear in the agricultural societies of the Near East and in Minoan Crete.

pieces.name: Hindenburg disaster
pieces.about: The Hindenburg disaster was an airship accident that occurred on May 6, 1937, in Manchester Township, New Jersey, U.S. The LZ 129 Hindenburg was a German commercial passenger-carrying rigid airship, the lead ship of the Hindenburg class, the longest class of flying machine and the largest airship by envelope volume. It was designed and built by the Zeppelin Company and operated by the German Zeppelin Airline Company. It was named after Field Marshal Paul von Hindenburg, who was president of Germany from 1925 until his death in 1934. Filled with hydrogen, it caught fire and was destroyed during its attempt to dock with its mooring mast at Naval Air Station Lakehurst. The accident caused 35 fatalities among the 97 people on board, and an additional fatality on the ground.

pieces.name: I have a Dream
pieces.about: "I Have a Dream" is a public speech that was delivered by American civil rights activist and Baptist minister Martin Luther King Jr. during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom on August 28, 1963. In the speech, King called for civil and economic rights and an end to racism in the United States. Delivered to over 250,000 civil rights supporters from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., the speech was one of the most famous moments of the civil rights movement and among the most iconic speeches in American history.

pieces.name: Attack on Pearl Harbor
pieces.about: The attack on Pearl Harbor was a surprise military strike by the Empire of Japan on the United States Pacific Fleet at its naval base at Pearl Harbor on Oahu, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. At the time, the U.S. was a neutral country in World War II. The air raid on Pearl Harbor, which was launched from aircraft carriers, resulted in the U.S. declaring war on Japan the next day. The Japanese military leadership referred to the attack as the Hawaii Operation and Operation AI, and as Operation Z during its planning.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon

pieces.name: The Last Supper
pieces.about: The Last Supper is the final meal that, in the Gospel accounts, Jesus shared with his apostles in Jerusalem before his crucifixion. The Last Supper is commemorated by Christians especially on Holy Thursday. The Last Supper provides the scriptural basis for the Eucharist, also known as "Holy Communion" or "The Lord's Supper".

pieces.name: Ancient Egypt
pieces.about: Ancient Egypt, civilization in northeastern Africa that dates from the 4th millennium BCE.

pieces.name: Renaissance
pieces.about: The Renaissance is a period of history and a European cultural movement covering the 15th and 16th centuries. It marked the transition from the Middle Ages to modernity and was characterized by an effort to revive and surpass the ideas and achievements of classical antiquity.

pieces.name: Spoon bending
pieces.about: Spoon bending is the deformation of objects, especially metal cutlery, purportedly by paranormal means. It is a common theme for magic tricks, which use a variety of methods to produce the effect. Performers commonly use misdirection to draw their audience's attention away while the spoon is manually bent. Another method uses a metal spoon that has been prepared by repeatedly bending the spoon back and forth, weakening the material. Applying light pressure will then cause it to bend or break.

pieces.name: Alchemy
pieces.about: A form of speculative thought that, among other aims, tried to transform base metals such as lead or copper into silver or gold. It also sought to discover cures for diseases and a way of extending life.

pieces.name: Apocalypse
pieces.about: The end of the world as people know it, or the collapse of a whole society, and what survivors build or lose afterward.

pieces.name: Apotheosis
pieces.sentence:
Chapter 20
Chapter 30

This concept refers to the potential divine nature and destiny of humans to ascend or transform into a higher state of being. In "The Lost Symbol," it ties into the Masonic belief in human potential and enlightenment, as well as the book’s exploration of the power of the human mind and spirit.
pieces.about: Apotheosis, also called divinization or deification, is the glorification of a subject to divine levels and, commonly, the treatment of a human being, any other living thing, or an abstract idea in the likeness of a deity. The original sense of apotheosis relates to religion and is the subject of many works of art.

pieces.name: Architecture
pieces.about: Architecture is the art and science of designing and constructing buildings, structures, and spaces that serve functional, aesthetic, and cultural purposes. It encompasses the planning, design, and execution of a wide range of projects, from individual homes to large-scale urban developments. Architects blend creativity, technical expertise, and practical considerations to create environments that enhance the quality of life for people and communities.

Dawn of the Planet of the Apes

pieces.name: Art
pieces.about:
Art is the expression or application of human creative skill and imagination, typically in a visual form such as painting or sculpture, producing works to be appreciated primarily for their beauty or emotional power.
Art is a dynamic and integral part of human culture and experience. It encompasses a wide range of forms and serves various functions, from personal expression to societal commentary. Understanding art involves appreciating its aesthetic qualities, recognizing its cultural significance, and engaging with its broader meanings and implications. Through art, we explore and express the complexities of the human condition, making it a vital and enduring aspect of our lives.

pieces.name: Astrology
pieces.about: Astrology is a range of divinatory practices, recognized as pseudoscientific since the 18th century, that propose that information about human affairs and terrestrial events may be discerned by studying the apparent positions of celestial objects.

pieces.name: Astronomy
pieces.about:
Astronomy is the scientific study of celestial objects, phenomena, and the universe as a whole. Astronomers seek to understand the origins, evolution, composition, structure, and behavior of celestial bodies such as stars, planets, moons, galaxies, and nebulae, as well as the fundamental laws and principles governing the cosmos.

Key aspects of astronomy include:

Observational Astronomy: Astronomers use telescopes, detectors, and other instruments to observe and study celestial objects and phenomena across the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves to gamma rays. Observational data provide insights into the properties, movements, and interactions of objects in space.
Theoretical Astronomy: Astronomers develop theoretical models, simulations, and mathematical frameworks to interpret observational data, make predictions, and test hypotheses about the nature and behavior of celestial objects and the universe as a whole. Theoretical astronomy encompasses fields such as astrophysics, cosmology, and planetary science.
Astrophysics: Astrophysics focuses on the physical properties and processes of celestial objects, including their formation, structure, composition, and evolution. Astrophysicists study phenomena such as stellar nucleosynthesis, stellar dynamics, black holes, gravitational waves, and the interstellar medium.
Cosmology: Cosmology is the study of the origin, evolution, and large-scale structure of the universe. Cosmologists investigate questions about the Big Bang theory, the expansion of the universe, dark matter, dark energy, cosmic microwave background radiation, and the ultimate fate of the cosmos.
Planetary Science: Planetary scientists study planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and other objects within our solar system and beyond. They investigate planetary geology, atmospheres, surfaces, interiors, and potential habitability, as well as processes such as impact cratering, volcanism, and planetary formation.
Astrobiology: Astrobiology explores the potential for life elsewhere in the universe, including the search for habitable environments, the origins of life on Earth, extremophiles, biosignatures, and the possibility of extraterrestrial life forms.

Astronomy is an interdisciplinary field that intersects with other branches of science, including physics, chemistry, biology, geology, and computer science. Astronomers collaborate with researchers from diverse disciplines to address complex questions about the universe and to advance scientific knowledge and understanding. Astronomy also inspires wonder, curiosity, and appreciation for the beauty and complexity of the cosmos, enriching human culture and civilization.

also.title: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: Atonement
pieces.about: Atonement, atoning, or making amends is the concept of a person taking action to correct previous wrongdoing on their part, either through direct action to undo the consequences of that act, equivalent action to do good for others, or some other expression of feelings of remorse.

pieces.name: Baptisms of the dead
pieces.about: Baptism for the dead is best known as a doctrine of the Latter Day Saint movement, which has practiced it since 1840. It is currently practiced by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church), where it is performed only in dedicated temples, as well as in several other current factions of the movement. Those who practice this rite view baptism as an essential requirement to enter the Kingdom of God, and therefore practice baptism for the dead to offer it by proxy to those who died without the opportunity to receive it.

pieces.name: Black magic
pieces.about: Black magic has traditionally referred to the use of supernatural powers or magic for evil and selfish purposes. The links and interaction between black magic and religion are many and varied

pieces.name: Body building
pieces.about: Bodybuilding is the practice of progressive resistance exercise to build, control, and develop one's muscles via hypertrophy. An individual who engages in this activity is referred to as a bodybuilder.

pieces.name: Body piercing
pieces.about: The piercing of holes in parts of the body other than the ear in order to insert rings, studs, or other pieces of jewelry. Body piercings have been used for spiritual and religious purposes for centuries. In some cultures, piercings are seen as a way to connect with a higher power, or to signify a connection to a particular faith. In many religions, piercings are seen as a way to symbolize a person's devotion to their faith.

pieces.name: Buddhism
pieces.about: Buddhism, also known as Buddha Dharma and Dharmavinaya, is an Indian religion and philosophical tradition based on teachings attributed to the Buddha. It is the world's fourth-largest religion, with over 520 million followers, known as Buddhists, who comprise seven percent of the global population.

also.title: A Tale for the Time Being

pieces.name: Bulimia nervosa
pieces.about:
Bulimia is a potentially life-threatening eating disorder.
People with this condition binge eat. They then take steps to avoid weight gain. Most commonly, this means vomiting (purging). But it can also mean excessive exercising or fasting.
Treatments include counseling, medications, and nutrition education.

pieces.name: Christianity
pieces.about: Christianity is an Abrahamic monotheistic religion based on the life and teachings of Jesus Christ. It is the world's largest and most widespread religion with roughly 2.4 billion followers, comprising around 31.2% of the world population.

also.title: Life During the Crusades
also.year: 1998 (Library of Congress record and copyright date c1998; Goodreads and some retailer listings say 1997 - see dropped.md)

pieces.name: Circumcision
pieces.about: A hood of skin, called the foreskin, covers the head (or glans) of the penis. In circumcision, the foreskin is surgically removed, exposing the end of the penis. Some families choose to circumcise based on cultural or religious beliefs. Others choose to for hygiene or appearance.

pieces.name: Claustrophobia
pieces.about: Claustrophobia is a fear of confined spaces. Claustrophobia is often caused by a traumatic event experienced during early childhood. For example, adults may develop claustrophobia if, as a child, they: were trapped or kept in a confined space. were bullied or abused.

pieces.name: Comparative religion
pieces.about: Comparative religion is the branch of the study of religions with the systematic comparison of the doctrines and practices, themes and impacts of the world's religions.

pieces.name: Conspiracy theory
pieces.about: A conspiracy theory is an explanation for an event or situation that asserts the existence of a conspiracy by powerful and sinister groups, often political in motivation, when other explanations are more probable.

pieces.name: Cosmetic surgery
pieces.about: Cosmetic surgery aims to improve how people look and feel about themselves. It can be performed on just about any part of the face or body.

pieces.name: Cosmic Consciousness
pieces.about: A term used to characterize a transcendence of the limits of self-consciousness. As an ultra-state of illumination of the mind, the roots of the conception are embodied in the quest for a spiritual connection with multi-dimensional cosmos. This quest searches for spiritual development as a pathway to human excellence, and can be associated with the mystics of ancient wisdom, as well as contemporary psycho-spiritual analysts.

pieces.name: Cosmology
pieces.about: Cosmology is a branch of physics and metaphysics dealing with the nature of the universe, the cosmos. Cosmology studies how the history of the universe led to the stars, galaxies, and other features we can observe today.

pieces.name: Cryptography and Decoding
pieces.about: Cryptography is the process of hiding or coding information so that only the person a message was intended for can read it. Decoding is the act, process, or result of extracting meaning or usable information, as from a code, written or spoken symbols, or an electronic signal

pieces.name: Daydream
pieces.about: A series of pleasant thoughts that distract one's attention from the present.

pieces.name: Death
pieces.about: Death is the end of life; the irreversible cessation of all biological functions that sustain a living organism. The remains of a former organism normally begin to decompose shortly after death. Death eventually and inevitably occurs in all organisms.

also.title: Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing

pieces.name: Dimension
pieces.about: In physics and mathematics, the dimension of a mathematical space is informally defined as the minimum number of coordinates needed to specify any point within it. Thus, a line has a dimension of one because only one coordinate is needed to specify a point on it – for example, the point at 5 on a number line.

pieces.name: Eidetic memory
pieces.about: Eidetic memory, also known as photographic memory and total recall, is the ability to recall an image from memory with high precision—at least for a brief period of time—after seeing it only once and without using a mnemonic device.

pieces.name: Entanglement theory
pieces.about: Quantum physics predicts that particles can become entangled. This suggests that two or more particles can be brought together and become fundamentally linked so that even when they're separated, even by great distances, it's no longer possible to describe them independently of each other.

pieces.name: ESP (Extrasensory perception)
pieces.about: Extrasensory perception, also known as a sixth sense, or cryptaesthesia, is a claimed paranormal ability pertaining to reception of information not gained through the recognized physical senses, but sensed with the mind. The term was adopted by Duke University botanist J. B. Rhine to denote psychic abilities such as intuition, telepathy, psychometry, clairvoyance, clairaudience, clairsentience, empathy and their trans-temporal operation as precognition or retrocognition.

pieces.name: Ethics
pieces.about: The study of right and wrong, and the principles that guide how people should act.

pieces.name: Exorcism
pieces.about: Exorcism is the religious or spiritual practice of evicting demons, jinns, or other malevolent spiritual entities from a person, or an area, that is believed to be possessed.

pieces.name: Experiment
pieces.about: An experiment is a procedure carried out to support or refute a hypothesis, or determine the efficacy or likelihood of something previously untried. Experiments provide insight into cause-and-effect by demonstrating what outcome occurs when a particular factor is manipulated.

also.title: How I Built This - Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales

pieces.name: Fairy tale
pieces.about: A fairy tale (alternative names include fairytale, fairy story, magic tale, or wonder tale) is a short story that belongs to the folklore genre. Such stories typically feature magic, enchantments, and mythical or fanciful beings.

pieces.name: Fasting
pieces.about: Fasting is abstention from eating and sometimes drinking. From a purely physiological context, "fasting" may refer to the metabolic status of a person who has not eaten overnight, or to the metabolic state achieved after complete digestion and absorption of a meal.

pieces.name: Fear
pieces.about: Fear is an intense emotional response to a perceived threat, danger, or harm. It triggers physiological and psychological reactions, including increased heart rate, sweating, trembling, and heightened alertness. Fear serves as a natural survival mechanism, preparing individuals to react to potential dangers by either confronting the threat or fleeing from it. However, excessive or irrational fear can lead to anxiety, avoidance behaviors, and impairments in daily functioning. Fear can arise from various sources, including real threats, imagined dangers, past traumas, and cultural influences.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
Journey to the Center of the Earth
One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest

pieces.name: Flight simulator
pieces.about: A flight simulator is a device that artificially re-creates aircraft flight and the environment in which it flies, for pilot training, design, or other purposes. It includes replicating the equations that govern how aircraft fly, how they react to applications of flight controls, the effects of other aircraft systems, and how the aircraft reacts to external factors such as air density, turbulence, wind shear, cloud, precipitation, etc. Flight simulation is used for a variety of reasons, including flight training (mainly of pilots), the design and development of the aircraft itself, and research into aircraft characteristics and control handling qualities.

pieces.name: Freemasonry
pieces.sentence:
Chapter 3
Chapter 118
The story is heavily centered around the Freemasons, a secret society with a rich history and complex rituals. The novel explores their symbols, rituals, and philosophies, particularly through the character of Peter Solomon, a high-ranking Mason. The secrets of the Freemasons are a driving force in the plot, with the antagonist, Mal’akh, seeking hidden Masonic knowledge that he believes will grant him great power.
pieces.about: Freemasonry or Masonry refers to fraternal organizations that trace their origins to the local guilds of stonemasons that, from the end of the 14th century, regulated the qualifications of stonemasons and their interaction with authorities and clients.

pieces.name: Gender transition
pieces.about: Gender transition is the process of affirming and expressing one's internal sense of gender, as opposed to the gender assigned to them at birth.

pieces.name: G-Force
pieces.about: The g-force or gravitational force equivalent is mass-specific force (force per unit mass), expressed in units of standard gravity (symbol g or g0, not to be confused with "g", the symbol for grams). It is used for sustained accelerations, that cause a perception of weight.

pieces.name: Heirloom
pieces.about: Something of special value handed down from one generation to another.

pieces.name: History
pieces.sentence:
Chapter 7
Chapter 30
The novel is set in Washington, D.C., and Dan Brown uses the city’s architecture and history to weave his narrative. Important locations like the Capitol, the Library of Congress, and the Washington Monument are integral to the plot. The story suggests that the city itself is filled with Masonic symbols and secrets waiting to be discovered.
pieces.about: History is the study of past events, particularly in human affairs, encompassing a wide range of disciplines, methodologies, and perspectives. It seeks to understand how societies, cultures, and individuals have evolved over time, influencing the present and shaping the future.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon

pieces.name: Human sacrifice
pieces.about: Human sacrifice was practiced in many human societies beginning in prehistoric times. Human sacrifice is the act of killing one or more humans as part of a ritual, which is usually intended to please or appease gods, a human ruler, public or jurisdictional demands for justice by capital punishment, an authoritative/priestly figure, spirits of dead ancestors or as a retainer sacrifice, wherein a monarch's servants are killed in order for them to continue to serve their master in the next life.

pieces.name: Ideology
pieces.about: Ideology, a form of social or political philosophy, or a system of ideas, that aspires both to explain the world and to change it.

pieces.name: Impartiality
pieces.about: Impartiality is a principle of justice holding that decisions should be based on objective criteria, rather than on the basis of bias, prejudice, or preferring the benefit to one person over another for improper reasons.

pieces.name: Incantation
pieces.about: A use of spells or verbal charms spoken or sung as a part of a ritual of magic

pieces.name: Inheritance
pieces.about: Money or property passed on to someone, usually after a death.

also.title: A Series of Unfortunate Events (TV series)
Lemony Snicket's A Series of Unfortunate Events

pieces.name: Initiation
pieces.about: The action of admitting someone into a secret or obscure society or group, typically with a ritual.

pieces.name: Inquisition
pieces.about: The Inquisition was a powerful office set up within the Catholic Church to root out and punish heresy throughout Europe and the Americas. Beginning in the 12th century and continuing for hundreds of years, the Inquisition is infamous for the severity of its tortures and its persecution of Jews and Muslims.

pieces.name: Journey
pieces.about: Traveling from one place to another, often over a long distance, and the experiences along the way that change a person - whether the trip is real or a passage through life.

also.title: Journey to the Center of the Earth
The Coffee Bean for Kids: A Simple Lesson to Create Positive Change
The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

pieces.name: Kabbalah
pieces.about: The ancient Jewish tradition of mystical interpretation of the Bible, first transmitted orally and using esoteric methods (including ciphers). It reached the height of its influence in the later Middle Ages and remains significant in Hasidism.

pieces.name: Knowledge
pieces.about: Facts, information, and skills acquired by a person through experience or education; the theoretical or practical understanding of a subject.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
How I Built This - Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales
Journey to the Center of the Earth

pieces.name: Legend
pieces.about: A legend is a genre of folklore that consists of a narrative featuring human actions, believed or perceived to have taken place in human history. Narratives in this genre may demonstrate human values, and possess certain qualities that give the tale verisimilitude.

pieces.name: Liquid breathing
pieces.about: Liquid breathing is a form of respiration in which a normally air-breathing organism breathes an oxygen-rich liquid, rather than breathing air, by selecting a liquid that can hold a large amount of oxygen and is capable of CO₂ gas exchange.

pieces.name: Magic
pieces.about: The power of apparently influencing the course of events by using mysterious or supernatural forces or mysterious tricks, such as making things disappear and appear again, performed as entertainment.

also.title: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

pieces.name: Mausoleum
pieces.about: A mausoleum is an external free-standing building constructed as a monument enclosing the burial chamber of a deceased person or people. A mausoleum without the person's remains is called a cenotaph. A mausoleum may be considered a type of tomb, or the tomb may be considered to be within the mausoleum.

pieces.name: Mindfulness
pieces.about: Mindfulness is the cognitive skill, usually developed through meditation, of sustaining meta-attention of the contents of one's own mind in the present moment.

pieces.name: Mind over matter
pieces.about:
“Mind over matter” is a simple expression that describes our ability to use our minds to self-regulate in the moment when situations or events seem out of our control. Emotions are brain-based, subjective, and conscious states of being that are the combination of four key elements: subjective experience, appraisal of the subjective experience, physiological arousal, and behavioral expression of the emotion.

The brain is a powerful emotion management tool. Under normal circumstances, people organize information and process experiences (also known as executive functioning) through the prefrontal cortex region of the brain, which is responsible for enabling us to have cognitive control of our behavior and for empowering us to select and successfully monitor behaviors that help us to achieve a chosen goal or a desired outcome.

pieces.name: Mythology
pieces.about: Myths as a subject: the stories a people tell about gods, heroes and how the world began, and what those stories mean.

pieces.name: National security
pieces.about: National security, or national defense, is the security and defense of a sovereign state, including its citizens, economy, and institutions, which is regarded as a duty of government.

pieces.name: Occult
pieces.about: occult, a term that was originally used in Latin to designate the hidden or unseen properties of things and that, since the 16th century, has also been used to characterize religious traditions that include belief in unseen forces or that otherwise behave in a secretive or mysterious manner. Moreover, in the phrase the occult, the term designates a range of religious traditions, typically of a culturally alternative or marginalized nature, that modern scholars more commonly categorize under the label esotericism.

pieces.name: Open-mindedness
pieces.about: Open-mindedness is receptiveness to new ideas. Open-mindedness relates to the way in which people approach the views and knowledge of others.

pieces.name: Patriot Act
pieces.about: The Patriot Act, or USA PATRIOT Act, was passed shortly after the terrorist attacks in the United States that occurred on September 11, 2001, and gave law enforcement agencies broader powers to investigate, indict, and bring terrorists to justice.

pieces.name: Philosophy
pieces.about: Philosophy is the systematic study of fundamental questions about existence, knowledge, reality, ethics, morality, reason, mind, and language. Philosophers engage in critical inquiry, analysis, and reflection to explore the nature of reality, the human condition, and the underlying principles that govern the universe

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
How I Built This - Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales
Journey to the Center of the Earth

pieces.name: Physics
pieces.about: Physics is the natural science of matter, involving the study of matter, its fundamental constituents, its motion and behavior through space and time, and the related entities of energy and force. Physics is one of the most fundamental scientific disciplines.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon

pieces.name: Pyramid
pieces.about: A pyramid is a structure whose visible surfaces are triangular in broad outline and converge toward the top, making the appearance roughly a pyramid in the geometric sense. The base of a pyramid can be of any polygon shape, such as triangular or quadrilateral, and its lines either filled or step.

pieces.name: Religion
pieces.about: Belief in God, gods or the sacred, and the faiths, practices and questions that come with it.

also.title: A Little History of the World
also.year: 1936 (German original, Eine kurze Weltgeschichte fuer junge Leser; English Wikipedia says it appeared in 1936, German Wikipedia says 1935 - see dropped.md; first English edition 2005)

also.title: The Story of the Trapp Family Singers

pieces.name: Rite of passage
pieces.about: A rite of passage is a ceremony or ritual of the passage which occurs when an individual leaves one group to enter another. It involves a significant change of status in society.

pieces.name: Ritual
pieces.about: A ritual is a sequence of activities involving gestures, words, actions, or revered objects. Rituals may be prescribed by the traditions of a community, including a religious community.

pieces.name: Sacrifice
pieces.about: Destruction or surrender of something for the sake of something else or something given up or lost.

also.title: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe

pieces.name: Sangreal/Holy Grail
pieces.about: Another term for the Grail; recorded from late Middle English, the word comes from Old French sant graal 'Holy Grail', although later spurious etymologies suggested that the original form was sang roial 'royal blood' or Sangreal, referring to the actual blood of Christ.

pieces.name: Science
pieces.about: The organized study of the natural world through observation, experiment and reasoning, and the knowledge it produces.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
A Red Herring Without Mustard: a Flavia de Luce mystery
Journey to the Center of the Earth

pieces.name: Science Vs. Religion
pieces.sentence: Throughout the novel, there is a tension between scientific understanding and religious belief. Katherine Solomon's work in noetic science attempts to bridge this gap, showing how science can intersect with spirituality, suggesting a convergence of science and religion in understanding human potential and consciousness.
pieces.about: One way to distinguish between science and religion is the claim that science concerns the natural world, whereas religion concerns the supernatural world and its relationship to the natural.

pieces.name: Scientific research
pieces.about: Research is the pursuit of new knowledge through the process of discovery. Scientific research involves diligent inquiry and systematic observation of phenomena. Most scientific research projects involve experimentation, often requiring testing the effect of changing conditions on the results.

also.title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks

pieces.name: Self-Control
pieces.about: Self-control—or the ability to manage one's impulses, emotions, and behaviors to achieve long-term goals.

pieces.name: Sensory deprivation
pieces.about: Sensory deprivation or perceptual isolation is the deliberate reduction or removal of stimuli from one or more of the senses.

pieces.name: Soul
pieces.about: The spiritual part of a person that is believed to give life to the body and in many religions is believed to live forever.

pieces.name: Stargate project
pieces.about: The Stargate Project was a secret U.S. Army unit established in 1977 at Fort Meade, Maryland, by the Defense Intelligence Agency and SRI International to investigate the potential for psychic phenomena in military and domestic intelligence applications.

pieces.name: Superstition
pieces.about: A widely held but unjustified belief in supernatural causation leading to certain consequences of an action or event, or a practice based on such a belief.

also.title: A Red Herring Without Mustard: a Flavia de Luce mystery

pieces.name: Superstring theory
pieces.about: Superstring theory is an attempt to explain all of the particles and fundamental forces of nature in one theory by modeling them as vibrations of tiny supersymmetric strings.

pieces.name: Surgical bilateral orchiectomy (Castration)
pieces.about: Castration is any action, surgical, chemical, or otherwise, by which a male loses use of the testicles: the male gonad. Surgical castration is bilateral orchiectomy, while chemical castration uses pharmaceutical drugs to deactivate the testes.

pieces.name: Symbology
pieces.sentence:
Chapter 3
The protagonist, Robert Langdon, is a symbologist, and his expertise is crucial throughout the novel. Symbols, codes, and cryptography are used to unravel mysteries and secrets. The plot involves deciphering an ancient Masonic Pyramid and a hidden capstone that contains encrypted information essential to the storyline.
pieces.about: The study of symbols

pieces.name: Symbology and Semiotics
pieces.about: Symbology refers to the analysis and understanding of symbols, a method of symbols as an instrument of transmission, while semiotics refers to the research and knowledge of signs. Semiotic studies are undertaken to understand the meaning and processes of characters, anything that communicates something.

pieces.name: Tattoo
pieces.about: A tattoo is a form of body modification made by inserting tattoo ink, dyes, and/or pigments, either indelible or temporary, into the dermis layer of the skin to form a design. Tattoo artists create these designs using several tattooing processes and techniques, including hand-tapped traditional tattoos and modern tattoo machines. The history of tattooing goes back to Neolithic times, practiced across the globe by many cultures, and the symbolism and impact of tattoos varies in different places and cultures.

also.title: A Series of Unfortunate Events (TV series)

pieces.name: Technology
pieces.about: Technology refers to the application of scientific knowledge, tools, and techniques to solve problems, improve efficiency, and enhance human capabilities. It encompasses a wide range of fields, including electronics, information systems, biotechnology, and engineering, and plays a crucial role in shaping modern society by advancing communication, healthcare, industry, and everyday life.

also.title: Journey to the Center of the Earth
Pope Leo's AI Warning, UFC at the White House, and CBS Shakeups
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: The Power of Ancient Wisdom
pieces.sentence: Ancient texts, symbols, and teachings are repeatedly referenced as holding timeless truths. The novel suggests that modern society has much to learn from ancient wisdom, particularly in understanding the human mind, spirit, and potential.
pieces.about: The body of knowledge and insights that were accumulated by human civilizations over thousands of years.

pieces.name: The Power of Thought
pieces.about: This power consists of your thoughts. The thoughts that pass through your mind are responsible for everything that happens in your life. Your predominant thoughts influence your behavior and attitude and control your actions and reactions. As your thoughts are, so is your life.

pieces.name: Thirty third degree (Freemasons)
pieces.about: Achieving the 33° is an honor that can be bestowed upon a Scottish Rite Mason. It is not campaigned for. It is granted solely by the Supreme Council. A 33° Mason is a Master Mason who has exhibited knowledge, passion and sacrifice to his craft. The Supreme Council awards the 33° as a way of honoring outstanding and selfless work performed in the Rite or in public life.

pieces.name: Torture
pieces.about: Torture is the deliberate infliction of severe physical or psychological pain and suffering upon a person, typically by a government or authority, for purposes such as punishment, coercion, interrogation, or intimidation. It involves the intentional use of violence, threats, or extreme measures to inflict harm and induce fear in the victim. Torture is universally condemned as a violation of human rights and international law, including the United Nations Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment.

pieces.name: Transformation
pieces.about: A thorough or dramatic change in form or appearance.

also.title: The Coffee Bean for Kids: A Simple Lesson to Create Positive Change

pieces.name: Treasure
pieces.about: Treasure is a concentration of wealth — often originating from ancient history — that is considered lost and/or forgotten until rediscovered. Some jurisdictions legally define what constitutes treasure, such as in the British Treasure Act 1996.

also.title: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: Trompe-l'œil
pieces.about: Trompe-l'œil is an artistic term for the highly realistic optical illusion of three-dimensional space and objects on a two-dimensional surface. Trompe l'œil, which is most often associated with painting, tricks the viewer into perceiving painted objects or spaces as real.

pieces.name: Wicca
pieces.about: A form of modern paganism, especially a tradition founded in England in the mid 20th century and claiming its origins in pre-Christian religions.

pieces.name: Deception
pieces.about: The act of causing someone to accept as true or valid what is false or invalid; the act of deceiving

also.title: A Red Herring Without Mustard: a Flavia de Luce mystery

pieces.name: Faith
pieces.sentence: The theme of faith, both in a religious and a broader spiritual sense, runs throughout the novel. Characters grapple with their beliefs in God, science, and the power of the human mind. The narrative suggests that faith can be a powerful force for good or evil, depending on how it is used and understood. The balance between faith and reason is a constant tension in the story.
pieces.about: Complete trust or confidence in someone or something.

also.title: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
The Old Man and the sea

pieces.name: Good and Evil
pieces.sentence: The novel explores the duality of good and evil, often suggesting that they are two sides of the same coin. Mal’akh, as the antagonist, embodies this duality—seeking enlightenment and power, but through dark and malevolent means. The Masonic ideals of wisdom and enlightenment contrast sharply with Mal’akh’s corruption and cruelty, highlighting the novel’s exploration of moral duality.
pieces.about: Good and evil are two opposing moral concepts that are used to describe actions, behaviors, and intentions. Good is associated with positive, beneficial, and virtuous qualities, while evil is associated with negative, harmful, and malevolent qualities.

also.title: Black Horse and the Cherry Tree
Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief
The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe
The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde

pieces.name: History
pieces.sentence: The novel frequently references historical events, figures, and philosophies, suggesting that the past has a profound influence on the present. The secrets of the Freemasons, embedded in American history and architecture, serve as a metaphor for how historical knowledge and wisdom continue to shape contemporary society. The story suggests that understanding history is crucial to understanding the present and the potential future.
pieces.about: History is the study of past events, particularly in human affairs, encompassing a wide range of disciplines, methodologies, and perspectives. It seeks to understand how societies, cultures, and individuals have evolved over time, influencing the present and shaping the future.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon

pieces.name: Human Potential
pieces.sentence: This theme is embodied in Katherine Solomon's work with noetic science, which explores the untapped potential of the human mind to affect physical reality. The novel suggests that humans have the capacity for great intellectual and spiritual achievements, and much of the plot revolves around unlocking this potential. This is also reflected in the Masonic philosophy of self-improvement and the apotheosis of man, or the idea that humans can ascend to a higher state of being.
pieces.about: Human potential is the capacity for humans to improve themselves through studying, training, and practice, to reach the limit of their ability to develop aptitudes and skills.

pieces.name: Knowledge and Discovery
pieces.sentence: The novel’s central plot revolves around a quest for hidden knowledge, particularly the secrets of the Freemasons. Characters like Robert Langdon and Peter Solomon are involved in a search for enlightenment, both personal and societal. The pursuit of knowledge, whether through ancient symbols, modern science, or esoteric traditions, is portrayed as a powerful and transformative journey.
pieces.about: The pursuit of understanding - learning, exploring, investigating or uncovering what was hidden - and what it gives and costs the people who seek it.

also.title: Journey to the Center of the Earth
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: Moral Decay and Corruption
pieces.sentence: The antagonist, Mal’akh, is driven by a desire for ultimate power and enlightenment through dark means. This theme explores how the pursuit of knowledge or power can lead to corruption and moral degradation. The novel contrasts this with the Masonic ideals of wisdom and self-betterment.
pieces.about: The gradual loss of moral values in a person or a society, often through greed, power or excess.

pieces.name: Morality
pieces.sentence: Characters in the novel often face ethical dilemmas and moral ambiguities. For example, Peter Solomon must decide how much of the Masonic secrets he can reveal to Robert Langdon and how to deal with the knowledge that could either enlighten or destroy. Mal’akh’s actions, though driven by a desire for enlightenment, are morally reprehensible, illustrating the fine line between the pursuit of knowledge and the descent into corruption.
pieces.about: Ideas of right and wrong behavior, and the values that guide a person's choices.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: Mysticism
pieces.sentence: The story delves into various forms of mysticism, including Kabbalah, Hermeticism, and other esoteric traditions that have influenced the Masons. These traditions often speak of hidden knowledge, spiritual enlightenment, and the power of symbols and words, all of which are themes in the story.
pieces.about: Mysticism is popularly known as becoming one with God or the Absolute, but may refer to any kind of ecstasy or altered state of consciousness which is given a religious or spiritual meaning.

pieces.name: Noetic Science
pieces.sentence: Noetic science, which studies the impact of human consciousness on the physical world, is a recurring theme. Katherine Solomon, a scientist in the field, conducts experiments that suggest human thoughts can influence matter. This idea is central to the novel’s exploration of the power of the mind and is linked to ancient wisdom and the mystical elements surrounding the Masons.
pieces.about: A multidisciplinary field of study that brings scientific tools and techniques together with subjective inner knowing to study the nature of reality.

pieces.name: Power of Symbols
pieces.sentence: The theme of symbolism is central to the narrative, with Robert Langdon, a symbologist, interpreting various symbols, codes, and ancient texts to unravel the mystery. The novel emphasizes that symbols have multiple layers of meaning and can be interpreted in various ways depending on the context and the observer's perspective. This theme also underscores the idea that truth is often hidden beneath layers of interpretation and requires careful analysis to uncover.

pieces.name: Science and Religion
pieces.sentence: The novel explores the relationship and tension between science and religion. Katherine Solomon’s noetic science is a key example, as it attempts to scientifically validate spiritual and metaphysical concepts. This theme is also reflected in the various symbols and texts that the characters decipher, which blend scientific principles with mystical and religious ideas, suggesting a convergence of the two realms in understanding the universe and human existence.
pieces.about: One way to distinguish between science and religion is the claim that science concerns the natural world, whereas religion concerns the supernatural world and its relationship to the natural.

pieces.name: Secrets
pieces.sentence: Secrecy is a pervasive theme, from the hidden rituals of the Freemasons to the confidential research conducted by Katherine Solomon. The novel suggests that some knowledge must be protected or concealed, either for the safety of the masses or to maintain power. The antagonist, Mal’akh, seeks to uncover and exploit these secrets for his own gain, which contrasts with the more altruistic motives of other characters.
pieces.about: A secret is something that is kept or meant to be kept unknown or unseen by others.

pieces.name: Self Discovery
pieces.sentence: Many characters in "The Lost Symbol" are on a journey of self-discovery. Robert Langdon’s quest is not only to solve a mystery but also to understand deeper truths about himself and his beliefs. Mal’akh, on the other hand, undergoes a darker form of self-discovery, driven by a desire to transcend his human limitations through transformation, which leads him to commit horrific acts.
pieces.about: Learning who one really is - one's strengths, beliefs and desires.

also.title: When I was little: A four-year-old's memoir of her youth.

pieces.name: The Secret Teachings of All Ages
Classical and modern cryptography for beginners
Archaeology
pieces.about: Archaeology is the scientific study of human history and prehistory through the excavation and analysis of artifacts, structures, and other physical remains. It aims to understand past human behaviors, cultures, and societies by examining material evidence. Archaeologists work in diverse environments, from ancient ruins and burial sites to underwater shipwrecks and urban areas.

also.title: Journey to the Center of the Earth
The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: Architecture
pieces.sentence: Bellamy’s role as the Architect of the Capitol places him in a unique position to understand the symbolic and historical significance of Washington, D.C.’s architecture, which is crucial to solving the novel’s puzzles. He uses his insider knowledge to help Langdon and Katherine.
pieces.about: Architecture is the art and science of designing and constructing buildings, structures, and spaces that serve functional, aesthetic, and cultural purposes. It encompasses the planning, design, and execution of a wide range of projects, from individual homes to large-scale urban developments. Architects blend creativity, technical expertise, and practical considerations to create environments that enhance the quality of life for people and communities.

also.title: Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs
Dawn of the Planet of the Apes

pieces.name: Archivist
pieces.about: An archivist is an information professional who assesses, collects, organizes, preserves, maintains control over, and provides access to records and archives determined to have long-term value. The records maintained by an archivist can consist of a variety of forms, including letters, diaries, logs, other personal documents, government documents, sound and/or picture recordings, digital files, or other physical objects.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs

pieces.name: Artist
pieces.about: An artist is a person who creates art (such as painting, sculpture, music, or writing) using conscious skill and creative imagination.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
A Tale for the Time Being

pieces.name: Civil Engineer
pieces.about: A civil engineer is a person who practices civil engineering – the application of planning, designing, constructing, maintaining, and operating infrastructure while protecting the public and environmental health, as well as improving existing infrastructure that may have been neglected.

also.title: Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs

pieces.name: Clergyman/Clergywoman
pieces.sentence: Galloway provides spiritual guidance and a deeper understanding of religious symbolism. His role as a dean also gives him insight into Masonic traditions, adding another layer to the novel’s exploration of faith, morality, and enlightenment.
pieces.about:
Clergy are formal leaders within established religions. Their roles and functions vary in different religious traditions, but usually involve presiding over specific rituals and teaching their religion's doctrines and practices. Some of the terms used for individual clergy are clergyman, clergywoman, clergyperson, churchman,
cleric, ecclesiastic, and vicegerent while clerk in holy orders has a long history but is rarely used.

also.title: The Canterbury Tales
also.year: 1992 (this audio recording, Recorded Books, release date 10/01/1992). The work itself was written 1387-1400 and first printed by William Caxton in 1476.

pieces.name: Conservator
pieces.about: A conservator-restorer is a professional responsible for the preservation of artistic and cultural artifacts, also known as cultural heritage. Conservators possess the expertise to preserve cultural heritage in a way that retains the integrity of the object, building or site, including its historical significance, context and aesthetic or visual aspects. This kind of preservation is done by analyzing and assessing the condition of cultural property, understanding processes and evidence of deterioration, planning collections care or site management strategies that prevent damage, carrying out conservation treatments, and conducting research. A conservator's job is to ensure that the objects in a museum's collection are kept in the best possible condition, as well as to serve the museum's mission to bring art before the public.

pieces.name: Consultant
pieces.sentence: Given the high-stakes environment and security concerns surrounding the Freemasons and government institutions, security consultants or experts would be involved in strategizing and implementing measures to protect sensitive information and locations.
pieces.about: A consultant is a professional who provides advice or services in an area of specialization. Consulting services generally fall under the domain of professional services, as contingent work.

pieces.name: Cryptographer
pieces.about: Cryptography, or cryptology, is the practice and study of techniques for secure communication in the presence of adversarial behavior. More generally, cryptography is about constructing and analyzing protocols that prevent third parties or the public from reading private messages. Modern cryptography exists at the intersection of the disciplines of mathematics, computer science, information security, electrical engineering, digital signal processing, physics, and others. Core concepts related to information security are also central to cryptography. Practical applications of cryptography include electronic commerce, chip-based payment cards, digital currencies, computer passwords, and military communications.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
Cracking the Luftwaffe Codes: The Secrets of Bletchley Park
Journey to the Center of the Earth
The Enigma Girls: How Ten Teenagers Broke Ciphers, Kept Secrets, and Helped Win World War II

pieces.name: Data Analyst
pieces.sentence: Nola Kaye, a systems analyst, plays a key role in analyzing data and interpreting evidence related to the unfolding crisis. Agent Simkins and other field agents are involved in tracking Langdon and protecting national security. Their roles reflect the intelligence community's efforts to manage potential threats.
pieces.about: A data analyst reviews data to identify key insights into a business’s customers and ways the data can be used to solve problems. They also communicate this information to company leadership and other stakeholders.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs

pieces.name: Detective
pieces.about: A detective's job is to identify, gather, and analyze evidence and facts surrounding various crimes… whether it’s a murder, kidnapping, arson or theft!

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
A Good Girl's Guide to Murder
A Red Herring Without Mustard: a Flavia de Luce mystery
Pete the Cat and the Missing Cupcakes
The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde

pieces.name: Director
pieces.sentence: As a wealthy philanthropist and the head of the Smithsonian Institution, Peter Solomon's career places him at the center of Washington, D.C.’s elite and within the Masonic community. His knowledge of artifacts and secret societies, combined with his influence, makes him a key figure in the plot.

also.title: Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope

pieces.name: Forensics agent
pieces.about: Forensic science, also known as criminalistics, is the application of science principles and methods to support legal decision-making in matters of criminal and civil law.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon

pieces.name: Geneticist
pieces.sentence: Given the novel’s references to human potential and transformation, a biologist or geneticist might explore the implications of Mal’akh’s beliefs in genetic enhancement or human evolution. The scientific exploration of human potential, especially in terms of noetic science and consciousness, aligns with the work of biologists and geneticists in understanding human capabilities.
pieces.about: A geneticist is a biologist or physician who studies genetics, the science of genes, heredity, and variation of organisms. A geneticist can be employed as a scientist or a lecturer. Geneticists may perform general research on genetic processes or develop genetic technologies to aid in the pharmaceutical or and agriculture industries. Some geneticists perform experiments in model organisms such as Drosophila, C. elegans, zebrafish, rodents or humans and analyze data to interpret the inheritance of biological traits. A basic science geneticist is a scientist who usually has earned a PhD in genetics and undertakes research and/or lectures in the field. A medical geneticist is a physician who has been trained in medical genetics as a specialization and evaluates, diagnoses, and manages patients with hereditary conditions or congenital malformations; and provides genetic risk calculations and mutation analysis.

pieces.name: Historian
pieces.sentence: Historians specializing in American history or Masonic history could provide context and background for the novel’s symbols and rituals.  Historians would play a role in uncovering the historical context of the Freemasons, Washington, D.C., and the ancient secrets embedded in the novel’s plot.
pieces.about: A historian is a professional who studies and interprets the past through research, analysis, and critical inquiry.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
A Little History of the World
also.year: 1936 (German original, Eine kurze Weltgeschichte fuer junge Leser; English Wikipedia says it appeared in 1936, German Wikipedia says 1935 - see dropped.md; first English edition 2005)

also.title: How I Built This - Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales
If I Could Turn Back Time
Life During the Crusades
also.year: 1998 (Library of Congress record and copyright date c1998; Goodreads and some retailer listings say 1997 - see dropped.md)

also.title: Percy Jackson & the Olympians: The Lightning Thief
Tupperware: The Promise of Plastic in 1950s America
Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: Intelligence Officer
pieces.about: Intelligence officers work for government agencies such as the CIA (Central Intelligence Agency), MI6 (Secret Intelligence Service), Mossad, or other national intelligence agencies. They collect and analyze information to provide insights on threats, risks, and opportunities to policymakers and decision-makers.

pieces.name: Librarian
pieces.sentence: Librarians or archivists at the Library of Congress or Smithsonian Institution would have access to historical documents and texts that could provide critical information for Langdon and the others. he preservation and accessibility of knowledge are key themes in the novel, making the role of librarians and archivists crucial in maintaining historical continuity and aiding research.
pieces.about: A librarian is a person who works professionally in a library providing access to information, and sometimes social or technical programming, or instruction on information literacy to users.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
A Red Herring Without Mustard: a Flavia de Luce mystery

pieces.name: Medical examiner
pieces.sentence: A medical examiner would likely be involved in analyzing Peter Solomon’s severed hand and other forensic evidence throughout the investigation. The presence of a medical examiner is crucial in understanding the methods and mindset of Mal’akh, adding depth to the investigation and providing details that guide the characters toward the truth.
pieces.about: The medical examiner is an appointed official in some American jurisdictions that investigates deaths that occur under unusual or suspicious circumstances, to perform post-mortem examinations, and in some jurisdictions to initiate inquests. They are necessarily trained in pathology.

pieces.name: Museum Curator
pieces.about: A museum curator is a person who works in a museum and is responsible for curating collections, exhibits and other artifacts that will be displayed at the museum. These professionals play a large role in how the museum's visitors experience the materials they see. Museum curators manage the collections and artifacts as well as care for them to ensure they maintain their integrity and condition.

also.title: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas

pieces.name: Pilot
pieces.sentence: Helicopter pilots are mentioned in scenes where characters are transported around Washington, D.C., especially in high-stakes moments involving the CIA and other authorities. Pilots are responsible for rapid transport and play a role in the logistical efforts to track down Mal’akh and respond to threats.
pieces.about: A person trained and licensed to fly an aircraft.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
Star Wars: Episode IV - A New Hope
The War That Saved My Life

pieces.name: Police Officer
pieces.sentence: Officer Nunez is involved in the initial response to the discovery of Peter Solomon’s severed hand in the Capitol Rotunda. His role represents the law enforcement perspective on the unfolding events and contributes to the urgency of the investigation.
pieces.about: Members of the department of government concerned primarily with maintenance of public order, safety, and health and enforcement of laws and possessing executive, judicial, and legislative powers

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
A Red Herring Without Mustard: a Flavia de Luce mystery
Dawn of the Planet of the Apes
When I was little: A four-year-old's memoir of her youth.

pieces.name: Professor
pieces.sentence: As a professor of symbology and religious iconology, Langdon’s expertise in interpreting symbols, codes, and ancient texts is central to solving the novel’s mysteries. His ability to decipher Masonic symbols and understand their historical context is critical in navigating the clues left by Peter Solomon and thwarting Mal’akh's plans.
pieces.about: Professor is an academic rank at universities and other post-secondary education and research institutions in most countries. Literally, professor derives from Latin as a "person who professes". Professors are usually experts in their field and teachers of the highest rank.

also.title: Bomb: The Race to Build and Steal the World's Most Dangerous Weapon
How I Built This - Wikipedia: Jimmy Wales

pieces.about:
Astronomy is the scientific study of celestial objects, phenomena, and the universe as a whole. Astronomers seek to understand the origins, evolution, composition, structure, and behavior of celestial bodies such as stars, planets, moons, galaxies, and nebulae, as well as the fundamental laws and principles governing the cosmos.

Key aspects of astronomy include:

Observational Astronomy: Astronomers use telescopes, detectors, and other instruments to observe and study celestial objects and phenomena across the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio waves to gamma rays. Observational data provide insights into the properties, movements, and interactions of objects in space.
Theoretical Astronomy: Astronomers develop theoretical models, simulations, and mathematical frameworks to interpret observational data, make predictions, and test hypotheses about the nature and behavior of celestial objects and the universe as a whole. Theoretical astronomy encompasses fields such as astrophysics, cosmology, and planetary science.
Astrophysics: Astrophysics focuses on the physical properties and processes of celestial objects, including their formation, structure, composition, and evolution. Astrophysicists study phenomena such as stellar nucleosynthesis, stellar dynamics, black holes, gravitational waves, and the interstellar medium.
Cosmology: Cosmology is the study of the origin, evolution, and large-scale structure of the universe. Cosmologists investigate questions about the Big Bang theory, the expansion of the universe, dark matter, dark energy, cosmic microwave background radiation, and the ultimate fate of the cosmos.
Planetary Science: Planetary scientists study planets, moons, asteroids, comets, and other objects within our solar system and beyond. They investigate planetary geology, atmospheres, surfaces, interiors, and potential habitability, as well as processes such as impact cratering, volcanism, and planetary formation.
Astrobiology: Astrobiology explores the potential for life elsewhere in the universe, including the search for habitable environments, the origins of life on Earth, extremophiles, biosignatures, and the possibility of extraterrestrial life forms.

Astronomy is an interdisciplinary field that intersects with other branches of science, including physics, chemistry, biology, geology, and computer science. Astronomers collaborate with researchers from diverse disciplines to address complex questions about the universe and to advance scientific knowledge and understanding. Astronomy also inspires wonder, curiosity, and appreciation for the beauty and complexity of the cosmos, enriching human culture and civilization.

pieces.sentence: Albert Einstein, a physicist; Erwin Schrödinger, a physicist; Isaac Newton, a physicist; Niels Bohr, a physicist; Robert Boyle, a physicist; Stephen Hawking, a physicist; Werner Heisenberg, a physicist.
pieces.about:
A physicist is a scientist who specializes in the study of the fundamental principles governing the behavior of matter, energy, space, and time. Physicists seek to understand the natural laws that govern the universe and use mathematical models, experimentation, observation, and theoretical analysis to explore and explain physical phenomena.

Key aspects of being a physicist include:

Theoretical Research: Physicists develop and refine theories, models, and mathematical frameworks to describe and predict the behavior of physical systems at various scales, from subatomic particles to the entire cosmos. They seek to uncover fundamental principles underlying the forces and interactions that shape the universe.
Experimental Investigation: Physicists design and conduct experiments to test hypotheses, verify theoretical predictions, and explore new phenomena. They use a variety of laboratory equipment, detectors, and instruments to measure physical properties and collect data, often collaborating with engineers and technicians to develop innovative experimental techniques.
Specialization: Physicists may specialize in various subfields of physics, such as particle physics, condensed matter physics, astrophysics, cosmology, quantum mechanics, relativity, nuclear physics, biophysics, or applied physics. Each subfield focuses on specific areas of inquiry and employs specialized methodologies and techniques.
Interdisciplinary Collaboration: Physicists frequently collaborate with researchers from other scientific disciplines, such as chemistry, biology, astronomy, engineering, computer science, and materials science. Interdisciplinary research projects often lead to new insights, discoveries, and applications across multiple fields.
Education and Outreach: Physicists engage in teaching, mentoring, and public outreach to share their knowledge and passion for physics with students, colleagues, and the general public. They may teach courses at universities, mentor graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, and participate in educational programs, science festivals, and public lectures.
Technological Innovation: Physicists contribute to technological advancements and innovations through research and development of new materials, devices, instruments, and technologies. Their discoveries and insights often have practical applications in fields such as telecommunications, electronics, healthcare, energy, and computing.

Physicists work in various settings, including universities, research institutions, government laboratories, private industry, and nonprofit organizations. They play a crucial role in advancing scientific knowledge, driving technological progress, and addressing complex challenges facing society, such as climate change, energy sustainability, and healthcare.

pieces.about:
A politician is an individual who is actively involved in politics, typically holding elected or appointed positions within government or political organizations. Politicians play a central role in shaping public policy, making decisions that affect society, and representing the interests of constituents or members of their political party.

Key aspects of being a politician include:

Public Service: Politicians are responsible for serving the public interest and addressing the needs and concerns of the communities they represent.
Policy Making: Politicians participate in the development, implementation, and evaluation of policies and legislation at local, regional, national, or international levels.
Campaigning: Politicians often engage in campaigning activities to seek election or re-election to public office, which may involve fundraising, canvassing, public speaking, and media outreach.
Representation: Politicians serve as representatives of their constituents or members of their political party, advocating for their interests, concerns, and priorities within government institutions.
Negotiation and Compromise: Politicians frequently engage in negotiation and compromise to build consensus, forge alliances, and advance their policy agendas in complex political environments.
Public Communication: Politicians communicate with the public through various channels, such as speeches, press releases, social media, and public appearances, to articulate their positions, explain policy proposals, and engage with constituents.

Politicians can hold a variety of positions, including:

Legislator: Serving in legislative bodies such as parliaments, congresses, or city councils, where they propose, debate, and vote on laws and policies.
Executive: Holding executive positions such as president, governor, mayor, or prime minister, where they oversee the implementation of laws and policies and manage government agencies and departments.
Judicial: In some systems, politicians may also hold judicial positions, such as judges or justices, responsible for interpreting and applying the law.
Party Leader: Leading political parties and shaping party platforms, strategies, and campaigns.

Politicians may belong to various political parties or movements, each with its own ideology, goals, and approaches to governance. They operate within legal and institutional frameworks, navigating political processes and dynamics to achieve their objectives and serve their constituents.

pieces.name: Field of study exploration!
pieces.sentence: Explore the field of noetic science by reading research articles or books from organizations like the Institute of Noetic Sciences (IONS). Participate in workshops or online courses that explore consciousness, the power of the mind, and the potential of human thought. Understanding the science of consciousness and the power of the mind adds depth to Katherine Solomon’s character and her research. It also ties into the novel’s theme of the potential of human thought and the intersection of science and spirituality.
pieces.about: Seek out information in various media formation about the field you wish to pursue.

pieces.name: Find the past in your world
pieces.sentence: Research and analyze the presence of Masonic and esoteric symbolism in modern pop culture, including movies, literature, music, and architecture. Understanding how Masonic symbols have permeated modern culture can offer insights into the continuing relevance of these symbols and their thematic significance in "The Lost Symbol."
pieces.about: Open your eyes, look around you. See how you can find the topics, themes and more, mentioned in the media, in your daily environment.

pieces.name: Get connected through history and architecture
pieces.sentence: Attend lectures, webinars, or museum exhibitions on American history, focusing on the architecture and symbolism of Washington, D.C., and other significant historical locations. This can provide historical context and insights into how the founding fathers and historical figures are portrayed in the novel, enhancing the appreciation of the thematic elements related to America’s foundation and Masonic influence.
pieces.about: Through multiple sensory stimuli touch, see, hear get acquainted with the architecture and history of a certain historical landmark.

pieces.name: Reading
pieces.sentence: Read books or take online courses on symbology, cryptography, or ancient symbols. Learning about the meanings and histories of different symbols can enhance understanding of Robert Langdon’s expertise and the symbolic clues scattered throughout the novel.
pieces.about: Find a book about a topic that interests you.

pieces.name: Solve Puzzles and Codes
pieces.sentence: Puzzles and codes are central to the novel's plot, and engaging in these activities can provide a sense of the excitement and challenge that Robert Langdon experiences. It also helps understand the intellectual thrill of solving complex problems.
pieces.about: Engage in puzzle-solving activities such as escape rooms, online cryptography games, or code-breaking apps. You can also try your hand at creating and solving your own ciphers and codes.

pieces.name: Talking together
pieces.sentence: Join a book club or online discussion group to talk about "The Lost Symbol" and its themes, characters, and plot. Engaging with others can provide different perspectives and interpretations. Discussing the novel with others can offer new insights and interpretations, helping to deepen understanding and appreciation of its complex themes and narrative structure.
pieces.about: Joining a discussion group can have many benefits. This groups can take place in person or online. You will find a great community of like-minded people to share ideas explored in the media.

pieces.name: Touring - visiting known landmarks
pieces.sentence: Take a guided tour or a self-guided exploration of the key locations mentioned in the novel, such as the U.S. Capitol, the Washington Monument, the Library of Congress, the Smithsonian Institution, and the Washington National Cathedral. Seeing these locations in person can help you visualize the settings described in the novel and understand the historical and architectural significance that Dan Brown emphasizes. Many of these sites also have Masonic symbols that are referenced in the novel.
pieces.about: Take a guided, or self-guided, tour.

pieces.name: Visit a lodge
pieces.sentence: Attend a lecture or visit a Masonic lodge open to the public to learn more about Freemasonry. Many cities have Masonic museums or libraries that offer exhibitions on Masonic history, symbols, and rituals. Gaining firsthand knowledge about Freemasonry can provide a deeper understanding of its influence on the novel’s plot and characters. This can also offer insights into the Masonic themes of enlightenment, secrecy, and the pursuit of knowledge.
pieces.about: Attend a lecture or visit a Masonic lodge open to the public to learn more about Freemasonry. Many cities have Masonic museums or libraries that offer exhibitions on Masonic history, symbols, and rituals.
